 ABC News News Home Ministers agree to huge school system shake-up and antisemitism plan Share Share article Ministers agree to huge school system shake-up and antisemitism plan
 By national education and parenting reporter Conor Duffy Topic: Education
 Posted Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 8:16am Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 8:16am Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 8:16am , updated Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 9:07am Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 9:07am Thu 5 Nov 2026 at 9:07am Education ministers have also agreed to a digital detox in schools. ( ABC News: Elise Pianegonda ) 
 In short:
 Education ministers met this week and agreed to reforms to address antisemitism and record-low civics scores.
 It is in response to Australia's lowest-ever scores in international and national tests.
 What's next?
 A new federal super commission will support teachers with the latest evidence-based practices.
 abc.net.au/news/education-ministers-agree-to-biggest-shake-up-in-years-of-school/107348312 Link copied Share Share article Australian students will learn about the "evils of antisemitism and the horrors of the Holocaust" from next year as part of new national curriculum resources developed in the wake of the Bondi Beach attack.
 Education ministers have endorsed the new resources designed by David Gonski's antisemitism education taskforce. They include more lessons about Jewish history and the contributions of Jewish Australians.
 "These changes are important but there is always more we can do to stamp out racism in all its noxious forms," Education Minister Jason Clare said. "The Social Cohesion Education Advisory Council, to be chaired by David Gonski AC, will progress further work to strengthen social cohesion through education."
 Ministers are also considering making civics and citizenship lessons mandatory in years nine and 10.
 'Quite shocking': Education experts sound alarm over worst ever civics scores
 National test results show just 28 per cent of Year 10 students are proficient in civics.
 Australian students recently recorded their worst-ever civics scores, with 72 per cent not understanding the basics of democracy. 
 "Schools don't just teach numeracy, literacy and critical thinking skills. They also build character," Mr Clare said.
 "We have to make sure our students are learning about our democracy and Australian values."
 Digital detox, federal super commission to tackle decline
 As ministers move to tackle 20 years of declining school results, they have agreed to establish an Australian Schools Digital Detox Taskforce as a backlash grows against screen time and education technology.
 Ministers have already agreed to return year five NAPLAN writing tests to paper and will now survey parents, students and teachers as they consider further reforms. 
 "Today we're announcing the next stage of reforms to help our kids learn and to support our teachers — a digital detox in schools restricting screen time and the use of AI," Mr Clare said.
 Warning Australia needs to lift NAPLAN performance
 NAPLAN test scores have revealed one-third of Australian students are not meeting "challenging but reasonable" expectations in literacy and numeracy.
 The reform comes as experts condemn Google over reports it plans to ban schools from using its search engine if they block the company's AI features. 
 "Schools should be able to limit generative AI when students need to do the thinking themselves," Swinburne University AI expert Atie Kia said.
 "They should not have to lose Google Search to make that choice."
 Education ministers have also agreed to a new national maths curriculum for the first three years of primary school as they battle NAPLAN scores showing one in three students not meeting minimum expectations in numeracy . 
 As part of the new curriculum, students will also be introduced to financial literacy.
 "[We're] strengthening the way we teach maths to the youngest students so they get this essential life skill," Mr Clare said.
 Loading... Ministers also agreed to establish a new Teaching and Learning Commission that would merge four existing education bodies.
 The commission will be responsible for the national curriculum, teacher standards, national testing and research on evidence-based teaching.
 "This will make it easier and simpler for teachers and schools to get the information, resources and support they need," Mr Clare said.
 The existing Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority (ACARA), Australian Institute for Teaching and School Leadership (AITSL), Australian Education Research Organisation (AER0) and Education Services Australia (ESA) will be brought together to form the new commission.
